subtopic_title: Estimation of capacity and mass of objects

text: Estimate the capacity of given objects.

record.content_text:
The SI unit for capacity is the litre. A capacity of one litre (1 L) is more or less equal to:

- six cups of tea
- a carton of milk
- three cans of soft drink.

Other units of measurement used often are multiples of ten of 1 L. The most common multiples are shown in the table below.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
      \hline
      \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Abbreviation} & \textbf{Size} & \textbf{Example} \\
      \hline
      \text{millilitre} & \text{ml} & 1\text{ ml}=\frac{1}{1,000}\text{ L}=0,001\text{ L} & \text{twenty drops of water } \\
      \hline
      \text{centilitre} & \text{cl} & 1\text{ cl}=\frac{1}{100}\text{ L}=0,01\text{ L} & \text{two teaspoons of water} \\
      \hline
      \text{kilolitre} & \text{kl} & 1\text{ kl}=1,000\text{ L} & \text{medium-sized inflatable swimming pool} \\
      \hline
      \end{array}
$$

closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.proposed_objective_text: Evaluate whether capacity and mass estimates are reasonable.
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.rationale: The textbook teaches learners to judge and correct capacity and mass estimates. That supports estimation but is distinct from producing an estimate for a given object.

closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.proposed_objective_text: Solve approximation word problems involving capacity and mass.
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.evidence_quote: Approximately how many bottles can be filled from the container?
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.rationale: These records require approximation calculations using capacity or mass. They are capacity/mass related, but they are not direct evidence for estimating the capacity or mass of a given object.
